name: prose-medium
description: A medium hand-written set of unique prose sentences (superset of prose_small)
samples: The morning light spilled across the kitchen table and made everything look briefly new.
She had always believed that small gestures carried more weight than grand pronouncements.
Rain tapped against the window in a rhythm that matched the old clock on the wall.
He reread the letter three times before he understood what it was really asking.
The garden grew wild that summer, full of weeds and unexpected flowers.
A good story changes the way you see the world even after you forget the details.
They walked to the edge of the field and stood in silence for a long while.
The coffee had gone cold, but neither of them wanted to move to make more.
Every city has a quiet hour just before dawn when it belongs to no one.
She kept the ticket stub in her wallet long after the trip was over.
He learned that patience was not waiting, but deciding not to hurry.
The library smelled of paper and dust and old decisions.
A sudden gust of wind sent the loose pages scattering across the lawn.
They built the boat in the garage over the course of one long winter.
Some questions are worth more than the answers they seem to demand.
The dog waited by the door, hopeful in a way only animals can be.
She wrote her name in the margin of the book, then regretted it immediately.
Evening arrived slowly, as if it was reluctant to commit to ending the day.
He could hear the river from his room most nights when the wind was right.
The best conversations happen when no one is trying to be impressive.
A single lantern hung at the end of the dock, swaying with the tide.
She had rehearsed the apology for a week and still said it all wrong.
The old farmhouse leaned slightly to one side, having long given up on being straight.
He counted the stars until his neck ached and then gave up somewhere past a hundred.
There is a particular loneliness that comes from being understood too quickly.
The pie crust was a disaster, but the filling made up for it entirely.
They argued about maps even though neither of them had any idea where they were.
Frost painted the window glass with delicate white ferns overnight.
She collected postcards of places she had never been and probably never would go.
The train slowed as it entered the station, sighing like a tired animal.
He found an old photograph of his grandmother and studied it for much longer than he expected.
The smell of bread drifted from the bakery and pulled a whole street toward it.
It is strange how a familiar smell can bring back an entire year in an instant.
They planted the tree on a cloudy day so it would not be shocked by the sun.
She kept switching between saying it was fine and saying it was not, and meant both.
The market on Saturday morning was loud, colorful, and completely impossible to rush through.
He wrote his best ideas down in the dark so he could forget them by daylight.
The river had carved the valley over millennia, patient as only stone can be.
A stranger smiled at her on the bus, and neither of them looked away first.
The snow swallowed the town's sound, leaving only the crunch of boots on the way home.
She had a habit of finishing other people's sentences, which did not endear her to everyone.
The lighthouse beam swept across the water every few seconds, a steady pulse in the dark.
He left the door unlocked that night, though he could not have explained why.
Some promises are made just to see how they feel in your mouth.
The kettle whistled, and with it the whole kitchen seemed to come to life.
They measured the year in seasons, not in days, and so it passed more gently.
She kept the letter unopened, certain that its contents would change things she was not ready to change.
The boy counted the steps from the road to the house until he knew them by heart.
A hawk circled high above the field, patient and patient again.
The piano in the corner was out of tune, but everyone pretended not to notice.
Midnight found her still at the desk, surrounded by half-finished things.
He had a way of making silence feel like agreement.
The station clock was always a little fast, as if it too was eager to move on.
She peeled the orange slowly, savoring the delay more than the fruit.
The old bridge groaned under the weight of morning traffic.
They named the stray cat after a city none of them had visited.
The letter she never sent still sits in a drawer like a held breath.
When he laughed, the whole room remembered how to breathe.
The tide drew back and left a mirror of sky on the wet sand.
She learned to bake in a kitchen too small for two, which taught her to share.
The summer ended the way summers do, all at once and without ceremony.
He kept a journal he never read, only wrote.
The curtains moved in the warm air, and for a moment the house seemed to sigh.
Trust, she decided, was just a willingness to be seen.
The last train of the night carried only the tired and the hopeful.
They buried the time capsule under the oak and forgot where the map was.
She hummed while she worked, a song she invented on the spot each morning.
The bookstore cat slept on the poetry section, approving of nothing in particular.
He learned more from the neighbor's silence than from anyone's advice.
The rain let up just long enough for the umbrellas to be pointless.
She had a drawer of buttons and no idea what she was saving them for.
The old radio played a song from the year they met, and the kitchen stopped.
He measured his life in books read and cups of tea, which was honest enough.
The fog rolled in like a quiet visitor who refused to leave.
She planted marigolds every spring, even though nothing in that soil ever bloomed well.
The crows gathered at dusk, gossiping in a language of wings.
He wrote thank-you notes for gifts he had not yet received, just in case.
The town wakes slowly in winter, reluctant to begin.
She learned to say no by first learning to say it quietly to herself.
The porch light stayed on all night, a small kindness to strangers.
He saved a seat for a friend who no longer lived in town.
The wind carried the sound of a distant train like a rumor.
She kept the seashell even after she forgot which beach it came from.
The apples in the bowl were wrinkled now, but still sweet.
He practiced the goodbye for weeks and still waved at the wrong moment.
The library's quiet settled over him like a familiar coat.
She had learned that you could lose something and keep it at the same time.
The kettle needed a new whistle, but they had grown fond of its sigh.
He counted the ceiling cracks into shapes and found a small dragon.
The first snow of the year always deserves a little ceremony.
She wrote letters in her head to people she would never send them to.
The baker's hands were flour-dusted, proof of a life spent making things warm.
He left a light on in the hallway, though the house was empty.
The river forgot nothing, though it forgave almost everything.
She learned to ride the bicycle with her hands off the handlebars, and then never needed to again.
The old songs came back to him at strange times, whole and uninvited.
They shared a single umbrella and got twice as wet, which was somehow the point.
The sunset lasted so long that it felt like a small rebellion.
He kept a list of favorite words and added to it only rarely, as if hoarding them.
The house settled at night with tiny creaks, adjusting itself to the dark.
She had a way of asking questions that made you tell the truth.
The ferry left the shore and the town grew small, then smaller.
He learned that some doors are opened by being left alone.
The market seller gave her an extra orange because she laughed at his joke.
She kept the program from the play, though she could not remember a single line.
The mountain held the snow late into spring, stubborn and beautiful.
He bought a compass he never used, liking the idea of always knowing north.
The children counted the days until summer on a chalkboard that grew smaller each evening.
She mended the quilt with mismatched thread, and it became her favorite thing.
The wind chime sang all night, and no one bothered to take it down.
He learned patience from a river that never seemed in a hurry.
The postcard said only wish you were here, and it meant it.
She kept a feather in her book as a marker and never did figure out whose.
The diner's clock was analog, and the wait, honest.
He taught himself to whistle and then spent a year putting it to use.
The garden's gate squeaked, a friendly warning that someone was coming.
She took the long way home whenever she needed time to think.
The paper lanterns floated up and away, carrying wishes like passengers.
He kept his grandmother's recipe in his own handwriting, adding notes no one asked for.
The pond froze over thin, and the children were not sure whether to risk it.
She learned home was a feeling, not a place, on a train going somewhere else.
The old dog knew the route better than the new driver and let it be known politely.
He planted a tree every birthday and could point to each year of himself.
The lighthouse keeper's log was full of ships that never passed.
She shared her umbrella with a stranger and they never spoke again, and it was perfect.
The seasons turned the fields gold, then brown, then patient.
He kept his first toolbox until the handles were smooth from his hands.
The bakery's doorbell had a particular chime that meant warm bread.
She wrote her resolutions in pencil, leaving room for change.
The smoke from the chimney made a small argument with the wind, and the wind won.
He learned that a good apology is a promise, not an explanation.
The harbor was quiet that night, full of small boats and bigger dreams.
She kept a habit of reading the last page first, so endings were never a surprise.
The oak tree held a tire swing that had outlived its first child.
He marked the doorframe with heights until the marks outnumbered the years.
The cobbler knew every pair of shoes in town by their owners' stories.
She walked the beach at low tide, collecting what the sea had decided to give up.
The lantern swung, and the shadows danced like old friends.
He kept a photograph of a house he had never owned, of a life he had imagined.
The birdsong started before dawn, outrageous and glorious and entirely unbothered.
She learned to fold paper cranes for no reason other than that her hands needed the work.
The snow fell straight down, without wind, as if the sky could not decide otherwise.
He kept the map folded the wrong way, comfortable in its creases.
The orphaned key sat on the table, a question no one remembered to answer.
She drank her tea before it cooled, a small act of decisiveness in a hesitant day.
The grandfather clock's chime was off by a minute, and the house forgave it.
He learned that leaving was sometimes the kindest thing you could hold on to.
The fire crackled and the room agreed to be quiet.
She kept a wildflower pressed in a book, a small piece of a day that mattered.
The journey turned out to be shorter than the goodbye, which surprised them both.
